summary: Describes sampling and filtering techniques for choosing which IP packets to look at, categorizes the common schemes, and lists the parameters needed to describe them. It also shows how simple selection methods can be combined into more elaborate ones. It provides the basis for the PSAMP work.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC sorts out the ways a router can pick the packets it reports for measurement. It separates sampling, which keeps a small representative share of the traffic, from filtering, which keeps only the packets that match a rule, and lists the settings each technique needs.

questions: how to select ip packets for measurement
subtitle: A catalogue of ways to pick the packets a measurement device reports.

tldr.problem: Measuring every packet on a busy link produces far more data than the measuring hardware, the storage and the network can carry, so some packets have to be left out.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sorts the selection techniques into sampling, which keeps a representative subset, and filtering, which keeps only packets with a given property, and defines the parameters needed to describe each scheme so that devices can be configured in a common way.
tldr.outcome: The document names the hash function that a compliant device must use for hash-based selection, lists the properties a hash function should have, and explains how the techniques can be combined into more elaborate selectors.

today: RFC 5475 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sits alongside RFC 5474, RFC 5476 and RFC 5477.

sections.title: Why Not Measure Every Packet
sections.content:
Two things drive the growth of measurement traffic. Network data rates keep rising, and the applications that use measurements want finer detail, so devices increasingly have to capture packet headers or parts of the payload and classify traffic for flow analysis. The result is an overwhelming amount of data, with high demands on resources for measurement, storage, transfer and post processing.

Specialized hardware can capture traffic at line rate, but its cost and the infrastructure needed to hold the measurements rule that out as a universal approach. Some form of data reduction at the point of measurement is therefore necessary, and this RFC looks at intelligent packet selection through sampling or filtering. Aggregation, which combines data into compact pre-defined views of the traffic, is a third way to reduce data and is out of scope here.

The two motivations differ. The purpose of sampling is to select a representative subset of packets so that estimates about the unsampled traffic can be made. The purpose of filtering is to remove all packets that are not of interest.
sections.plainLanguage: A fast link produces more packets than anyone can store or process. A measuring device has to throw most of them away, and this RFC describes the two ways to do that: keep a fair share of the traffic, or keep only what matches a rule.

sections.title: The Vocabulary of Packet Selection
sections.content:
An Observation Point is a place in the network where packets can be seen, such as a line with a probe attached, a shared medium, a router port or set of interfaces, or a measurement subsystem inside an interface. One observation point may be a superset of others, since a whole line card contains the interfaces on it. The Observed Packet Stream is every packet seen at that point, and the Packet Content is the union of the packet header, which carries the link, network and other encapsulation headers, and the payload. At some observation points the link header is not available.

A Selection Process takes the observed packet stream as its input and selects a subset of it as its output. It may keep a Selection State, such as packet sequence numbers, a timestamp of observation, iterators for pseudorandom number generators, hash values, or indicators of whether a packet was selected. A Selector defines what the process does with a single packet, using the packet content, information about how the packet was treated at the observation point, or the selection state. A Composite Selector is an ordered composition of selectors, where the output of one becomes the input of the next; a selector that is not composite is primitive. The Selection Sequence is a unique value per observation domain describing the observation point and the selector identifiers involved.

The Metering Process selects packets and produces a Report Stream of packet reports and report interpretation. The Exporting Process bundles reports into export packets and sends them to a Collector. A PSAMP Device hosts at least one observation point, a metering process and an exporting process, typically colocated at a router.
sections.plainLanguage: The document names each part of the process: where packets are seen, the rule that picks some of them, the state the rule keeps between packets, and the machinery that ships the results onwards.

sections.title: Sampling and Filtering Are Different
sections.content:
Sampling targets a representative subset of packets, used to infer knowledge about the whole observed set without processing it all. The selection can depend on packet position, on packet content, or on random decisions. Filtering selects a subset with common properties, used when only some packets are of interest. Filtering is deterministic: it depends on the packet content or on how the router treated the packet, and never on packet position or on a random decision.

Hashing sits between the two. Computing a hash over some bits of the packet header or content and selecting the packet when the value falls in a chosen range is deterministic on the content, so by this categorization it is a filtering technique. Yet hash functions are sometimes used to imitate random sampling, and depending on the input bits, the function and the selection range, the technique can emulate random selection with a given probability. It is also a powerful way to select the same packet subset at several observation points.

The categorization in the RFC marks each scheme for determinism and content dependence. Only schemes that are both content dependent and deterministic count as filters.
sections.plainLanguage: Sampling keeps a fair share of the traffic so you can estimate the rest. Filtering keeps only what matches a rule. Hashing counts as filtering, even when it is used to imitate a random choice.

sections.title: The Sampling Schemes
sections.content:
Systematic sampling picks the start points and the length of the selection intervals by a deterministic function, for example every k-th packet, or all packets that arrive at set times. The risk is bias: if the pattern of the sampler resembles a pattern in the traffic being measured, the estimate is likely to be biased, and the pattern in the traffic may not be known in advance. Only equally spaced schemes are considered here: triggers that are periodic in time or in packet count, with all packets in the interval selected.

Random sampling picks the starting points with a random process, so that each choice is an independent experiment and unbiased estimates are possible. In n-out-of-N sampling, n elements are chosen out of a population of N, for example by generating n random numbers in the range [1,N] and selecting the packets at those positions; the sample size is fixed. In probabilistic sampling, each element is selected with a given probability, so the sample size can vary between trials.

Probabilistic sampling is uniform when every packet has the same probability p, which in the count-driven form is called geometric random sampling, because the gap between selected packets has a geometric distribution with mean 1/p; the time-driven version, exponential random sampling, has exponentially distributed gaps. Non-uniform probabilistic sampling lets the probability depend on the packet, which boosts the chance of picking rare but important packets; unbiased estimators are recovered by re-normalizing the sample values. A third variant, non-uniform flow state dependent sampling, depends on the state of the flow the packet belongs to and on the other flows being monitored, and is used together with an IPFIX metering process.
sections.plainLanguage: Sampling comes in a few shapes. A systematic sampler takes everything between fixed points in time or in packet count. A random sampler flips a coin for each packet, so the sample size varies. Some samplers raise the odds for packets that matter more, such as rare ones.

sections.title: The Two Filtering Techniques
sections.content:
Filtering is the deterministic selection of packets based on the packet content, on how the packet was treated at the observation point, or on deterministic functions of these held in the selection state. A packet is selected when these quantities fall into a specified range. Unlike sampling, the decision never depends on the position of the packet in time or space, nor on a random process.

Property match filtering selects a packet when specific fields in the packet, or properties of the router state, equal a predefined value. The fields can be any of the IPFIX flow attributes. Several filters can be combined with AND by concatenating them, and the result does not depend on the order, though the order matters for implementation, since the first filter has to work at a higher rate. OR operations are not supported in this basic model and need vendor-specific schemes. The router state that can be filtered on includes the ingress and egress interfaces, whether the packet violated an Access Control List, a failed Reverse Path Forwarding check, a failed Resource Reservation Protocol check, the absence of a route, and the origin or destination Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) autonomous system. Because encryption hides the real values of encrypted fields, the filter must be able to ignore encrypted packets when it detects them.

Hash-based filtering maps the packet content, or part of it, onto a hash range, and selects the packet when the result falls in the hash selection range. Its main use is coordinated packet selection: the same packets are selected at different observation points. That is useful for following the path a packet took through the network, for passive one-way delay measurements, and for generating pseudorandom numbers where computing resources are scarce. The method only works across observation points if they all use the same hash function with the same parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: Filtering has two forms. One matches a field or a router condition, such as the packet arriving on a given interface. The other computes a hash of the packet and keeps it when the result falls in a chosen range, which lets several routers pick the same packets.

sections.title: Choosing a Hash Function
sections.content:
The hash function should have six properties. Speed, because it is applied to every packet that passes the observation point. Uniformity, so that a small change in the input spreads widely over the output range and the attained selection fraction stays close to the configured one. Unbiasedness, so that the selected packets are not skewed towards one type. Representativeness of the sample. Non-linearity, which improves mixing and reduces predictability. And robustness against attacks. For digesting packet content into a label, a low collision frequency matters most, followed by accepting variable-length input; speed is of secondary importance there because only selected packets are digested.

Ideally a cryptographically strong hash function with a private parameter in pseudorandom function mode would be used. No single function meets all the requirements, and the strong ones are slow: the computation times for MD5 and SHA are about 7 to 10 times higher than for non-cryptographic functions, and the difference grows for short inputs. Not every device can apply such a function to every packet at line rate.

For packet selection the BOB function MUST be used to be compliant with PSAMP, and its initial value and selection range should be kept private, with the initial vector configured out of band so it is not exposed. CRC-32 and IPSX MAY be used; with CRC-32 the input should first be post-pended with a private string and the modulus kept private. IPSX is simple and was about an order of magnitude faster per packet than BOB or CRC-32, but it is limited to 16 bytes of input. For digesting, BOB SHOULD be used and CRC-32 MAY be used; IPSX is not recommended for digesting because of its higher collision rate and its fixed-length input.

With BOB and IPv4 traffic, the input bytes must be the IP identification field, the flags field, the fragment offset, the source and destination IP addresses, and a configurable number of payload bytes from a configurable offset. With IPv6 traffic they must be the payload length, bytes 10, 11, 14, 15 and 16 of the source and destination addresses, and again a configurable number of payload bytes, with at least 4 recommended. All the hash functions evaluated were evaluated only for IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC requires the BOB hash function for packet selection, with a private starting value, and allows CRC-32 and the simpler IPSX as well. The input has to be the same at every router on the path, so fields that change hop by hop are left out.

sections.title: Describing and Combining Techniques
sections.content:
Every technique is described with three things: a unique identifier for the selector, a selector type, and the parameters for it. For sampling, the type is one of systematic count-based, systematic time-based, random n-out-of-N, uniform probabilistic, non-uniform probabilistic, or non-uniform flow state. The parameters depend on the type: population size N and sample size n for n-out-of-N; interval length and spacing in microseconds for systematic time-based; interval length and spacing in packets for systematic count-based; the sampling probability p for uniform probabilistic; and a calculation function for the probability for non-uniform probabilistic sampling.

For filtering, the types are matching, hashing and router state. Matching needs an information element and a value, with several match criteria bound by a logical AND. Hashing needs the hash domain, which is given as the input bits from the packet: for IPv4 a sequence of 20 hexadecimal numbers forming a 20-byte bitmask over the header, for IPv6 a sequence of 40 hexadecimal numbers forming a 40-byte bitmask, plus the number of payload bytes and a bitmask for them. It also needs the hash function name, the length of the input key, the output value with its length and bitmask, and the hash selection range given as a list of non-overlapping intervals. Router state filtering lists the same conditions as property match filtering.

Techniques can be composed by listing several selector identifiers in one selection sequence. When a filter comes before a sampling process, it splits one stream into several parent populations that can each be sampled with their own parameters, which allows a more accurate tuning. When filtering follows sampling, the same fraction applies to the whole stream, and packets that the filter would drop still load the sampler. So filtering first is more accurate, but sampling first may be needed when the filter is too complex to run at line rate. Stratified sampling goes further: the parent population is divided into subsets by a characteristic that is known to correlate with the one being estimated, and each subset is sampled separately, which raises the accuracy for the same sample size or shrinks the sample needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each technique is written down as a name, a type and a list of settings. Techniques can be chained, and a filter placed before the sampler usually gives a more accurate estimate, because each group of traffic can be sampled at its own rate.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main concern with hash-based selection is that a large set of related packets could be sampled far more often than the configured rate, either because the hash function behaves unexpectedly or because the packets were crafted to have that property. A hash function with good mixing properties helps, and its statistical properties should be evaluated on up-to-date traces from the network where it will be deployed.

An attacker who knows the hash function can craft packets that are known to be selected. Without a private input parameter, an attacker can compute the hash of any packet in advance, and by hashing trial packets can build a large set of packets that are either all selected or all not selected, whatever the strength of the function. With a private parameter, the risk remains if the function is not cryptographically strong: CRC-32 has weak mixing for low-order bits, so incrementing the hash input gives distinct packets whose hashes mostly fall in a narrow range. A cryptographically strong function with a private parameter in pseudorandom function mode is not vulnerable to these attacks, even when the selection range is known.

Knowledge of selection outcomes helps an attacker. It can be gained from billing reports, from feedback through an intrusion detection system, or by watching the report stream on a public network, even when the export packets are encrypted, because the occurrence of packets can be correlated with the crafted traffic. Padding export packets to a constant length and sending them at a constant rate removes that correlation. With a modular hash, knowing the outcomes of roughly 2/p packets is enough to succeed, and more outcomes reveal the parameters. Because hash-based selection is deterministic, packets with known selection properties can also be replayed; changing the hash parameters regularly limits this, and the change must happen at about the same time at every observation point to keep trajectory sampling working.

Other points: a user can learn the start and stop triggers of time-based systematic sampling by sending test packets, and adjust their sending schedule to be selected more or less often. Random sampling should use a cryptographically strong random number generator so that an advisory cannot predict the decision. Threats from configuring and reporting the sampling parameters cannot be assessed here, since those methods are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a hash always gives the same answer for the same packet, someone who knows the hash can craft packets that are always picked, or always skipped. Keeping the hash's starting value secret and using a strong hash function makes that much harder.

viz.caption: CATEGORIZATION OF THE SELECTION SCHEMES IN SECTION 4
THE PROPERTIES A HASH FUNCTION SHOULD HAVE

items.title: Speed
items.text: It runs on every packet that passes the observation point.

items.title: Uniformity
items.text: Small input changes spread widely over the output range.

items.title: Unbiasedness
items.text: The selected packets are not skewed towards one type.

items.title: Representativeness
items.text: The sample looks like the traffic it came from.

items.title: Non-linearity
items.text: The function is not linear, which improves mixing and hides patterns.

items.title: Robustness
items.text: The function resists attacks that craft packets to be selected.

viz.caption: THE NAMES THE RFC GIVES TO EACH PART

items.title: Observation Point
items.text: The place in the network where packets are seen.

items.title: Observed Packet Stream
items.text: All the packets seen at that point.

items.title: Selection Process
items.text: The part that takes the stream and picks a subset of it.

items.title: Selector
items.text: The rule applied to one packet at a time.

items.title: Selection State
items.text: What the process remembers between packets.

items.title: Composite Selector
items.text: Several selectors chained, each feeding the next.

items.title: Metering Process
items.text: The selection plus the production of reports.

items.title: Exporting Process
items.text: The part that ships the reports to a Collector.
